title: Three Buttons
statement: A calculator shows the number $1$ and has exactly three buttons: one multiplies the number shown by $2$, one multiplies it by $3$, and one multiplies it by $5$. A student presses the buttons one at a time until the calculator shows $180$. Every number shown after a press must be even. How many different sequences of button presses are possible?
hints: Write $180$ as a product of primes. What does this tell you about how many times each button must be pressed?

Since $180 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, the buttons used are fixed and only their order can vary. Counting orders in which some items are identical is a problem of permutations with repetition, but first you must work out which orders the evenness rule allows.

The first press shows $2$, $3$ or $5$, so it must be the $2$-button. An even number stays even when multiplied by any whole number, so the rule places no restriction on later presses. Now count the orders of the four presses $2, 3, 3, 5$, where swapping the two $3$-presses gives the same sequence.
solution: Each press multiplies the number shown by $2$, $3$ or $5$, so the final number is the product of the numbers on the buttons pressed. Since $180 = 2^2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$ and prime factorisation is unique, every valid sequence has exactly two presses of the $2$-button, two of the $3$-button and one of the $5$-button. Conversely, any order of these five presses gives $180$. The number shown increases with every press, so $180$ first appears on the last press and the student does not stop early. The first press shows the number on the button itself, so it must be the $2$-button, because $3$ and $5$ are odd. After that the number shown is even, and an even number multiplied by a whole number is still even. Hence every later number is automatically even, and the rule restricts only the first press. The other four presses are one $2$, two $3$s and one $5$, in any order. There are $4$ positions for the $2$-press, then $3$ remaining positions for the $5$-press, and the two $3$-presses must fill the last two positions in just one way. This gives $4 \cdot 3 = 12$ orders, which agrees with $\frac{4!}{2!} = 12$. The number of possible sequences is $12$. Why this works. permutations-with-repetition, prime-factorization: the factorisation fixes which presses occur, so once the first press is forced, only the orders of the remaining presses with a repeated $3$ need counting.
